title: Professional Skills, Lesson 3: Preparing for the timed coding test and the case interview
subtitle: Time management, the order in which you build a solution, and how to think out loud while working
whyItMatters: The timed coding test is the real screening round for almost every engineering role. Most candidates fail it not for lack of knowledge but for mismanaging time - and that is something you can train.
openingQuestion: In a 90-minute coding test, what should you do first?
openingOptions: Start writing code immediately to make the most of the time available in the test
Read the whole brief, identify the deliverable, then allocate the hours
Optimise the hard algorithmic part first because it carries the most marks
Set up the folder structure, linter and code formatting before writing the first line
explanation: The most common way candidates fail is by building the early parts meticulously and running out of time before the program runs end to end. A rough solution that runs and passes the main test cases always scores higher than a beautiful half-finished one, because the employer wants to know whether you can deliver under time pressure. Reading the brief first and working backwards from the deliverable is the simplest technique there is, and the most frequently skipped.

diagram.label: Read the brief, identify the final deliverable
Allocate the time backwards across each section
Write a working version first, refine afterwards
Keep the last 10 minutes for running the tests and writing notes

realWorldExample.description: The brief: build a small API that reads an orders file, totals the amount per customer and returns the result. The first candidate designs an elaborate data layer, writes error handling for every case, and runs out of time just as file reading is finished. The second writes a simple version that runs the whole flow from reading the file to returning the result, with a few test cases, and then uses the remaining time to go back, handle malformed data and note the assumptions. The second candidate is chosen almost every time, even though their error handling is cruder.

quiz.question: What is the principle for writing code under time pressure?
options: Copy the structure from a template project prepared before the test
Perfect each section as far as possible before moving to the next
Prioritise the core algorithm and skip reading the input data if short of time
Write a simple end-to-end working version first, then refine each part
quiz.explanation: This approach guarantees you have something submittable at any moment, and it also surfaces integration errors between parts early - the very errors that a part-by-part approach only reveals when it is far too late. Perfecting sequentially is what leaves candidates stranded, skipping the input handling means nothing actually runs, and a memorised template rarely fits the brief in front of you.

quiz.question: Why should you think out loud in an observed case exercise?
options: Because the assessor grades the reasoning, and silence shows them nothing
Because the interview process requires candidates to narrate every single action
Because speaking aloud helps the candidate catch errors in their own arithmetic
Because the assessor needs notes on the steps to compare candidates with each other
quiz.explanation: A candidate who reaches a wrong answer with coherent reasoning usually scores higher than one who reaches the right one and cannot explain why. It is not a procedural requirement and it is not primarily about catching your own slips or about the assessor's note-taking. In real work you always have to defend your solution, not merely produce it.

quiz.question: When a piece of information is missing from the brief, what is the right way to handle it?
options: Stop and ask the examiner until you receive an exact answer
State your assumption clearly, note it in the code, and carry on
Skip the part that needs the information and move on to other sections
Pick any interpretation since the aim is to complete the program structure
quiz.explanation: Missing information in a brief is usually deliberate, to see how you cope with incomplete requirements - exactly as in real work. Waiting for the examiner burns the clock, skipping the section leaves the program unconnected, and picking an interpretation at random is only different from a stated assumption in one respect, which is the one that matters. Stating the assumption openly is the right answer; quietly choosing an interpretation and saying nothing is the wrong one.

quiz.question: What should most of the final 10 minutes be spent on?
options: Add several extra minor features so the solution looks more complete
Reformat the code and harmonise naming conventions across files
Rerun the tests, sweep for errors, and write a few notes on the solution
Recheck all the input-reading code written at the start of the exercise
quiz.explanation: A program that does not run or fails a basic test case is rejected outright no matter how good the rest is. Extra features and tidy formatting add nothing when the core is unverified, and rereading the input code at that point is the least likely place for a fatal error. A few lines of notes also show you understand what trade-offs your solution makes - the part most candidates drop when the clock runs out.

quiz.question: Why do employers accept a rough but working solution?
options: Because they assume the candidate will be trained further after joining
Because a rough solution is easier to grade, saving the panel time
Because code polish does not matter much in real day-to-day work
Because it proves the candidate can deliver a finished product on time
quiz.explanation: In real work, deadlines are real and always earlier than you would like. Code quality does matter on the job, grading convenience is not a design goal of the exercise, and nobody is counting on post-hire training to supply the basics. The ability to break work down so that a usable version always exists is a core professional skill, and the test is designed to measure exactly that.

keyTakeaways: Read the whole brief and allocate time backwards from the deliverable before typing the first line of code
Write an end-to-end working version first and refine later - do not perfect one section at a time
When information is missing, state the assumption clearly and note it; do not quietly pick one
Keep the last 10 minutes for rerunning the tests and writing a few notes

practicePrompt.question: With 20 minutes left, your processing step is not yet wired to the output step and two test cases are failing. What should you do?
options: Keep fixing until every case is right, accepting no time for the output step
Note what is unfinished, use a simple workaround to run on and produce a result
Delete the failing test cases so the submission looks clean, then submit
Stop and explain to the assessor that the task is too long for the time given
practicePrompt.explanation: The assessor needs to see you carry the whole flow through to a final result. An honest note saying the wiring is incomplete and this is the temporary workaround shows you have the situation under control. Deleting the failing test cases is the worst option of the four - it conceals rather than acknowledges.

summary.keyIdea: The test measures your ability to deliver under pressure, not the sophistication of the code
summary.commonMistake: Pouring time into the opening sections and running out before producing a final answer
summary.action: Time yourself for 90 minutes solving a brief that builds a small API with tests, and repeat it three times with three different briefs.

application.title: A four-week practice plan
application.message: Week 1: solve briefs with no time limit until the structure is second nature. Week 2: time yourself at 120 minutes. Week 3: 90 minutes. Week 4: 90 minutes while narrating your reasoning out loud, as though someone were watching.
application.secondary: The skill here is closer to sport than to academic study - it comes from the number of repetitions, not the number of pages read.

sections.text: Lesson 1 taught you to write a design doc; lesson 2 taught you to defend a proposal. This lesson is about the situation where writing code and explaining it are tested at once against a countdown clock, and about why most people who fail do not fail on knowledge.

items: 10 minutes: read the brief, identify the deliverable, sketch the structure and write down the assumptions
20 minutes: write the input-reading part at the simplest acceptable level
30 minutes: write the core processing and wire it to input and output until the whole flow runs
20 minutes: write tests for the main cases and one or two edge cases
10 minutes: sweep for errors, rerun the tests, write short notes

sections.label: The working-version principle
sections.text: At any point in the 90 minutes you should have a program that runs end to end, differing only in how polished it is. This is exactly the minimum viable product principle, and for the same reason: it protects you from running out of time with something half-built.

left.label: What you think is being graded
left.text: How optimal the algorithm is and how thoroughly every error case is handled.

right.label: What is actually being graded
right.text: Whether the structure is clean, whether the parts connect correctly, how you handle missing information, and whether you reach a result inside the deadline.

sections.title: Checking the clock mid-way through a 90-minute test
sections.task: The plan splits 90 minutes into five parts (10, 20, 30, 20, 10 minutes). You have finished the first three parts with the actual times below. Print each part with its actual time, cumulative time and lateness against the plan's cumulative mark, then a last line: minutes left, minutes the last two parts need, and the shortfall. The starter code compares each part on its own, so it misses accumulated lateness.
sections.expectedOutput:
Read the brief: 12/10 min, total 12/10 - late 2
Input: 22/20 min, total 34/30 - late 4
Core processing: 41/30 min, total 75/60 - late 15
15 min left, last two parts need 30 min: short by 15
hints: Lateness is actual cumulative minus planned cumulative, not actual minus plan for that part alone.
The shortfall is the minutes the last two parts need minus the minutes left.

sections.title: How the 90 minutes are split
sections.caption: The suggested allocation in this lesson for a 90-minute test, not a rule of any particular exam. Note that testing and error review still get their own slots, because running out of time with an unfinished product is a common reason for failing.

s.text: You are on a 90-minute coding test. Reading the data and the main processing both run, with 45 minutes left. The prompt is missing one detail on how fees are calculated. What do you do?

choices.label: Stop everything until you can ask the proctor
Write down a clear assumption, say it aloud, and continue
Guess silently and just write it, telling the grader nothing

a.text: The proctor only repeats the prompt and you lose ten minutes. There is no time left to join the pieces and do the final check, so the program does not run end to end.

c.text: The grader sees the output and cannot tell which assumption you chose or why. A reasonable choice becomes an unexplained guess.

b.text: The grader nods, seeing you state the assumption. With 20 minutes left you have two options: handle a rare error case, or make sure the program runs end to end and tidy variable names. Which?

choices.label: Make it run end to end, tidy names, keep the last 10 minutes for review
Handle the rare error case right up to the last minute of the test

d.text: You submit a working program with clean structure and stated assumptions. Recruiters accept a rough solution that runs over an elaborate one that is unfinished.

e.text: You finish the rare case but two parts are not joined properly and the print step has a bug. What is graded is structure and integration, not the rare case.

lines: The timed coding test does not measure knowledge; it measures working habits under pressure.
The final lesson of the stage steps back to view all of these skills within a career path.
